prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Italian newspapers, an archbishop and civil liberties campaigners expressed shock and revulsion on Monday after photographs were published of sunbathers apparently enjoying a day at the beach just meters from where the bodies of two drowned Roma girls were laid out on the sand. Photographs of the dead Roma girls on a beach caused outrage in Italy. Italian news agency ANSA reported that the incident had occurred on Saturday at the beach of Torregaveta, west of Naples, southern Italy, where the two girls had earlier been swimming in the sea with two other Roma girls. Reports said they had gone to the beach to beg and sell trinkets. Local news reports said the four girls found themselves in trouble amid fierce waves and strong currents. Emergency services responded 10 minutes after a distress call was made from the beach and two lifeguards attended the girls upon hearing their screams. Two of them were pulled to safety but rescuers failed to reach the other two in time to save them.  Watch why the photos have generated anger » . The Web site of the Archbishop of Naples said the girls were cousins named Violetta and Cristina, aged 12 and 13. Their bodies were eventually laid out on the sand under beach towels to await collection by police. Photographs show sunbathers in bikinis and swimming trunks sitting close to where the girls' feet can be seen poking out from under the towels concealing their bodies. A photographer who took photos at the scene told CNN the mood among sunbathers had been one of indifference. Other photos show police officers lifting the bodies into coffins and carrying them away past bathers reclined on sun loungers. "While the lifeless bodies of the girls were still on the sand, there were those who carried on sunbathing or having lunch just a few meters away," Italian newspaper La Repubblica reported. Corriere della Sera said that a crowd of curious onlookers that had formed around the bodies quickly dispersed. "Few left the beach or abandoned their sunbathing. When the police from the mortuary arrived an hour later with coffins, the two girls were carried away between bathers stretched out in the sun." The incident also attracted condemnation from the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Crecenzio Seppe. "Indifference is not an emotion for human beings," Seppe wrote in his parish blog. "To turn the other way or to mind your own business can sometimes be more devastating than the events that occur." Recent weeks have seen heightened tensions between Italian authorities and the country's Roma minority amid a crackdown by Silvo Berlusconi's government targeting illegal immigrants and talk by government officials of a "Roma emergency" that has seen the 150,000-strong migrant group blamed for rising street crime. That has provided justification for police raids on Roma camps and controversial government plans to fingerprint all Roma -- an act condemned by the European Parliament and United Nations officials as a clear act of racial discrimination. Popular resentment against Romanies has also seen Roma camps near Naples attacked and set on fire with petrol bombs by local residents. In a statement published on its Web site, the Italian civil liberties group EveryOne said Saturday's drowning had occurred in an atmosphere of "racism and horror" and cast doubt on the reported version of events, suggesting that it appeared unusual for the four girls to wade into the sea, apparently casting modesty aside and despite being unable to swim. "The most shocking aspect of all this is the attitude of the people on the beach," the statement said. "No one appears the slightest upset at the sight and presence of the children's dead bodies on the beach: they carry on swimming, sunbathing, sipping soft drinks and chatting." CNN's Jennifer Eccleston contributed to this report.

**(CNN) —** Italian newspapers, an archbishop, and civil liberties campaigners expressed shock and revulsion on Monday after photographs emerged of sunbathers apparently enjoying a day at the beach just meters from where the bodies of two drowned Roma girls lay on the sand.

The photographs of the girls’ bodies on the beach sparked outrage across Italy.

The incident occurred Saturday at Torregaveta beach, west of Naples in southern Italy, according to the Italian news agency ANSA. The two girls had been swimming in the sea with two other Roma girls. Reports said they had gone to the beach to beg and sell trinkets.

Local news outlets reported that the four girls ran into difficulty amid fierce waves and strong currents. Emergency services responded 10 minutes after a distress call was made from the beach, while two lifeguards went to the girls’ aid after hearing their screams. Two were pulled to safety, but rescuers were unable to reach the other two in time.

*Watch why the photographs have generated anger »*

The website of the Archbishop of Naples identified the girls as cousins named Violetta and Cristina, ages 12 and 13. Their bodies were eventually laid out on the sand beneath beach towels while awaiting collection by police.

Photographs show sunbathers in bikinis and swimming trunks sitting near the bodies, with the girls’ feet visible beneath the towels. A photographer who took pictures at the scene told CNN that the prevailing mood among sunbathers was one of indifference.

Other photographs show police officers placing the bodies in coffins and carrying them away past bathers reclining on sun loungers.

“While the lifeless bodies of the girls were still on the sand, there were those who carried on sunbathing or having lunch just a few meters away,” the Italian newspaper *La Repubblica* reported.

*Corriere della Sera* said that a crowd of curious onlookers that had gathered around the bodies quickly dispersed.

“Few left the beach or abandoned their sunbathing. When the mortuary police arrived an hour later with coffins, the two girls were carried away between bathers stretched out in the sun.”

The incident also drew condemnation from the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Crescenzio Sepe.

“Indifference is not an emotion for human beings,” Sepe wrote on his parish blog. “To turn the other way or to mind your own business can sometimes be more devastating than the events that occur.”

Recent weeks have brought heightened tensions between Italian authorities and the country’s Roma minority amid a crackdown by Silvio Berlusconi’s government targeting illegal immigrants. Government officials have also spoken of a “Roma emergency,” with the 150,000-strong migrant group blamed for rising street crime.

That rhetoric has been used to justify police raids on Roma camps and controversial government plans to fingerprint all Roma—a measure condemned by the European Parliament and United Nations officials as a clear act of racial discrimination.

Popular resentment toward Romanies has also led local residents to attack Roma camps near Naples and set them on fire with petrol bombs.

In a statement published on its website, the Italian civil liberties group EveryOne said Saturday’s drowning had occurred in an atmosphere of “racism and horror.” The group also questioned the reported account of events, suggesting that it seemed unusual for the four girls to wade into the sea, apparently setting aside concerns about modesty despite being unable to swim.

“The most shocking aspect of all this is the attitude of the people on the beach,” the statement said. “No one appears the slightest upset at the sight and presence of the children’s dead bodies on the beach: they carry on swimming, sunbathing, sipping soft drinks and chatting.”

CNN’s Jennifer Eccleston contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Italian media outlets, a senior Catholic cleric and civil rights advocates reacted with horror on Monday after images emerged showing beachgoers apparently continuing to relax only a few meters from the bodies of two Roma girls who had drowned.

The photographs, taken on a beach in Italy, provoked widespread outrage. According to the Italian news agency ANSA, the tragedy happened on Saturday at Torregaveta beach, west of Naples in southern Italy. The two victims had entered the sea with two other Roma girls. Reports said the four had gone to the beach to beg and sell small ornaments.

Local media reported that powerful waves and strong currents left the girls in difficulty. Emergency personnel arrived 10 minutes after a call for help was placed from the beach, while two lifeguards responded after hearing the girls’ cries. Two of the four were rescued, but the other two could not be reached soon enough.

The website of the Archbishop of Naples identified the victims as cousins Violetta and Cristina, ages 12 and 13. Their bodies were placed on the beach and covered with towels while they awaited removal by police.

In the images, people wearing bikinis and swimming trunks can be seen sitting near the bodies, with the girls’ feet visible beneath the towels. A photographer who documented the scene told CNN that the other beachgoers appeared largely unconcerned. Additional pictures show officers putting the bodies into coffins and carrying them past people still lying on sun loungers.

La Repubblica reported that some people continued eating lunch or sunbathing only a short distance away while the children’s bodies remained on the sand.

Corriere della Sera said a group of curious spectators initially gathered around the scene but soon broke up. According to the newspaper, hardly anyone left the beach or stopped sunbathing. About an hour later, mortuary police arrived with coffins, and the girls’ bodies were taken away through rows of people still stretched out in the sunshine.

Cardinal Crecenzio Seppe, the Archbishop of Naples, also denounced the reaction. Writing on his parish blog, Seppe said indifference was not a human emotion and warned that ignoring events or focusing only on one’s own affairs could sometimes be more destructive than the incident itself.

The deaths occurred during a period of growing friction between Italy’s authorities and its Roma population. Silvo Berlusconi’s government had launched a campaign against undocumented immigrants, while officials spoke of a “Roma emergency” and blamed the country’s approximately 150,000 Roma migrants for increasing street crime.

Those claims were used to support police raids on Roma settlements and disputed plans to take fingerprints from every Roma person. The European Parliament and United Nations officials condemned the proposal as an unmistakable form of racial discrimination.

Public hostility toward Romanies had also led residents near Naples to attack Roma camps and set them ablaze with petrol bombs.

EveryOne, an Italian civil liberties organization, said in a statement on its website that the drownings had taken place in a climate of “racism and horror.” The group also questioned the official account, arguing that it seemed strange that the four girls would have entered the water despite being unable to swim and while apparently disregarding customary modesty.

The organization said the most disturbing feature was the conduct of those present on the beach. It noted that no one seemed visibly troubled by the children’s bodies and that people continued swimming, tanning, drinking soft beverages and talking.

CNN’s Jennifer Eccleston contributed to the report.

**Outrage in Italy as beachgoers sunbathe near bodies of drowned Roma girls**

**NAPLES, Italy** — Images of holidaymakers continuing to sunbathe just meters from the covered bodies of two Roma girls who drowned near Naples have sparked outrage across Italy and renewed debate over discrimination against the country’s Roma community.

The girls, ages 12 and 13, drowned while swimming off a public beach at Torregaveta, west of Naples. Emergency workers placed their bodies on the sand and covered them with towels as authorities carried out their investigation.

Photographs published by Italian newspapers showed beachgoers lying under umbrellas, talking and relaxing nearby. The apparent indifference prompted condemnation from politicians, religious leaders and commentators, who said the scene reflected a troubling lack of compassion.

Italy’s political establishment called for the tragedy to be treated with dignity, while the Vatican newspaper *L’Osservatore Romano* described the response on the beach as a sign of moral numbness.

Some witnesses said rescuers had tried to save the girls and that many people may not initially have understood what had happened. But the images quickly became a symbol of wider tensions surrounding Roma migrants, who have long faced poverty, segregation and hostility in Italy.

The deaths came amid a government crackdown on unauthorized Roma settlements and growing public concern about immigration and crime. Human-rights advocates warned that increasingly hostile rhetoric had helped dehumanize an already marginalized population.

For many Italians, the most disturbing aspect of the tragedy was not only that two children had died, but that ordinary life on the crowded beach appeared to continue around them.

counterfactuals.output:
**Roma Girls’ Drowning Near Naples Exposes Italy’s Deepening Ethnic Divide**

**TORREGAVETA, Italy —** The bodies of two young Roma girls lay beneath beach towels at the edge of the sand while, only a short distance away, holidaymakers continued to sunbathe.

The girls, widely identified in Italian media as Cristina and Violetta, aged about 12 and 13, drowned after entering rough water off Torregaveta, a seaside community west of Naples. Two other girls who were swimming with them were rescued, but emergency workers were unable to revive Cristina and Violetta.

Photographs from the beach quickly became the defining images of the tragedy. In them, the girls’ covered bodies remained on the shoreline awaiting removal as people sat under umbrellas, talked and rested nearby. The images provoked outrage across Italy and abroad, with commentators asking whether such apparent indifference would have been possible had the victims not been Roma.

Witness accounts differed over the response on the beach. Some people reportedly helped alert rescuers, and officials cautioned that the photographs did not show everything that happened before or after the drownings. Yet for Roma advocates, the scene captured a broader reality: a minority community living on the margins of Italian society and increasingly portrayed as a public-order threat.

The drownings came amid a forceful government campaign targeting unauthorized Roma settlements and street crime. Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi’s center-right administration had declared a security emergency in several regions, including Campania, the region surrounding Naples. Authorities conducted raids on informal camps, dismantled settlements and began compiling information about residents.

The most contentious proposal involved identifying and fingerprinting people living in Roma camps, including children. Government officials said the census was needed to establish who lived in the settlements, identify undocumented migrants and ensure that children attended school. Interior Minister Roberto Maroni defended the policy as an administrative and protective measure rather than an ethnic registry.

Human-rights organizations, opposition politicians and Roma representatives rejected that explanation. They argued that singling out one ethnic community for fingerprinting revived some of Europe’s darkest historical practices and risked treating Roma children as presumptive criminals. European institutions also demanded assurances that Italy would comply with anti-discrimination rules and protections for minors.

The dispute unfolded in an atmosphere of intense public anxiety over immigration and crime. Roma people—an ethnically diverse population that includes Italian citizens as well as migrants from Romania and the former Yugoslavia—were often discussed as though they were a single foreign group. Politicians and sections of the media repeatedly linked Roma settlements to theft, begging and urban disorder.

That rhetoric had tangible consequences. In the Naples area, mobs had attacked and burned Roma camps after allegations that a Roma woman had attempted to abduct a child. Residents fled as makeshift homes were destroyed. Rights monitors said the violence demonstrated how quickly accusations against an individual could become collective punishment against an entire community.

Roma families also faced entrenched barriers unrelated to criminality: substandard housing, limited access to education and health care, unemployment and frequent evictions. Many lived in officially designated or informal camps isolated from the surrounding population. Advocates said those policies reinforced segregation while allowing authorities to describe the resulting poverty as evidence that Roma people were unwilling to integrate.

Against that backdrop, the deaths of Cristina and Violetta took on significance beyond an accidental drowning. Italian newspapers debated the behavior of the beachgoers and the moral meaning of the photographs. Some saw a society numbed by suffering; others warned against condemning everyone present on the basis of a single image. But few disputed that the girls died at a moment when hostility toward Roma people had become unusually visible.

Catholic leaders and civil-rights groups called for the children to be remembered first as victims, not as symbols or members of a stigmatized group. They urged authorities to investigate the circumstances of the drowning while confronting the prejudice exposed by the public reaction.

The government maintained that its security measures were directed at illegal settlements and undocumented residents, not at Roma ethnicity. Critics countered that when raids, registries and political rhetoric overwhelmingly affect one minority, the distinction becomes difficult to sustain.

On the beach at Torregaveta, the ordinary rituals of summer continued around two covered bodies. For many Italians, that juxtaposition became an accusation in itself—a stark image of how exclusion can make even the death of a child appear distant.
